extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (TC 2100) drafting 35 U.S.C. §103 obviousness rejections
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for patent examiners on applying KSR and Graham v. John Deere principles to support prima facie obviousness rejections under 35 U.S.C. §103, including a set of rationales (A–G) and the factual findings required for each rationale. Emphasizes proper factual support, mapping claim limitations to prior art, and drafting clear rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graham v John Deere factors must be articulated
rubrics_metrics.description: Graham v John Deere is still the controlling case on obviousness and all 103 rejections must show a reasoned Graham v Deere analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EVERY rejection under 35 USC 103 must convey the Graham v Deere Factors. In particular, ensure a clear articulation of the Graham factors in both ordinary 103 rejections and obvious-type double patenting rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear articulation of reasons supporting obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: A key to supporting any rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103 is the clear articulation of the reasons why the claimed invention would have been obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide facts and reasoning in accordance with Examination Guidelines for Determining Obviousness; merely including conclusory statements in an Office action is insufficient to establish a prima facie case and to shift the burden to Applicant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching-Suggestion-Motivation (TSM) Test
rubrics_metrics.description: The TSM Test is a valid approach but not the only way to determine obviousness; a good TSM rejection will preempt most hindsight arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Findings for TSM: 1) What A teaches; 2) What A doesn't teach; 3) What B teaches; 4) What is the level of skill in the art; 5) Why it would have been obvious to modify reference A with B including a teaching, suggestion, or motivation. B may be official notice or part of the base reference; motivation need not come from the reference itself. When using 3+ references, state what AB doesn't teach, what C teaches, and why combine C with AB.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combining prior art elements using known methods to yield predictable results
rubrics_metrics.description: All claimed elements were known in the prior art and one skilled in the art could have combined the elements as claimed by known methods with no change in their respective functions and the combination would have yielded predictable results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Findings required: 1) Prior art included each claimed element (not necessarily in a single reference); 2) One of ordinary skill could have combined the elements by known methods and each element would perform the same function as separate; 3) One of ordinary skill would have recognized the results of the combination were predictable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple substitution of one known element for another
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim would have been obvious because the substitution of one known element for another would have yielded predictable results to one of ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Findings: 1) Prior art contained a device/method differing from the claimed invention by substitution of components; 2) The substituted components and their functions were known in the art; 3) One of ordinary skill could have substituted one known element for another and the results would have been predictable. Note: no motivation as to why to swap is needed. Caution: combining elements is not sufficient if results would not have been predictable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of a known technique to improve similar devices in the same way
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim would have been obvious because the technique for improving a particular class of devices was part of the ordinary capabilities of a person of ordinary skill, given teaching of the technique in other situations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Findings: 1) Prior art contained a 'base' device upon which the claimed invention is an improvement; 2) Prior art contained a comparable device that was improved in the same way; 3) One of ordinary skill could have applied the known improvement technique to the base device and the results would have been predictable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applying a known technique to a known device ready for improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim would have been obvious because a particular known technique was recognized as part of the ordinary capabilities of one skilled in the art and the base device was ready for improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Findings: 1) Prior art contained a 'base' device upon which the claimed invention is an improvement; 2) Prior art contained a known technique applicable to the base device; 3) One of ordinary skill would have recognized that applying the known technique would have yielded predictable results. Not necessarily limited to the same field of invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: "Obvious to try" — finite predictable solutions with reasonable expectation of success
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim would have been obvious because one skilled in the art had good reason to pursue known options within technical grasp; if this led to anticipated success, it is likely ordinary skill rather than invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Findings: 1) A recognized problem or need in the art (including design need or market pressure); 2) A finite number of identified predictable potential solutions; 3) One of ordinary skill could have pursued known potential options with a reasonable expectation of success. Example: choosing an LRU cache algorithm from a short list of replacement strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Known work in one field prompting predictable variations in same or different field (market/design incentives)
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim would have been obvious because design incentives or market forces provided a reason to make an adaptation and the invention resulted from applying prior knowledge in a predictable manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Findings: 1) Prior art scope included a similar or analogous device (same or different field); 2) Design incentives or market forces would have prompted adaptation; 3) Differences between the claimed invention and prior art were encompassed in known variations or known principles; 4) One of ordinary skill, in view of incentives/forces, could have implemented the variation and it would have been predictable. Evidence of market forces should be made of record; if notoriously well-known, Official Notice may be taken.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art is broader than applied references (includes POSITA understanding and common understanding)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art is not limited just to the references being applied but includes the understanding of one of ordinary skill in the art, and the common understanding of the layman.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners may rely on official notice, common sense, design choice, and ordinary ingenuity as part of prior art/context. However, factual findings supporting reliance should be made of record when feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiners may rely on official notice, common sense, design choice, and ordinary ingenuity
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners may rely on official notice, common sense, design choice, and ordinary ingenuity, for example, when supporting obviousness conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Official notice may be used for notoriously well-known facts; otherwise provide record evidence. The motivation for a modification need not always appear in the references themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Map claim limitations to pertinent sections of prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiner is to map all the claim limitations to the pertinent sections of the prior art references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When drafting a rejection, explicitly indicate which portions of each reference disclose each claim limitation; slides illustrate mapping but do not provide a full exposition of the rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: When using three or more references, articulate incremental gaps and combination rationale
rubrics_metrics.description: When writing a 103 rejection using 3 or more references, include what AB doesn't teach, what C teaches, and why it would be obvious to combine C with AB.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Add necessary steps showing the absence in prior combinations and the specific teachings of additional references that fill those gaps and the rationale for combining them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide record evidence for factual findings (market forces, predictability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence should be made of record to support the factual findings, such as those regarding market forces; if it is notoriously well known, Official Notice may be taken of that fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document support (citations, references, data) when asserting market forces, predictability, or other factual bases; rely on official notice only for truly notorious facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conclusions must be factual and reasoned; no unsupported conclusory statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Merely including conclusory statements in an Office action is insufficient to establish a prima facie case of obviousness and therefore insufficient to shift the burden to Applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the rejection contains factual findings and reasoning in line with Examination Guidelines (MPEP 2141). A well-reasoned rejection with factual support is more important than selecting a particular rationale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select the rationale(s) with the strongest explicit support
rubrics_metrics.description: One should pick the rationale or a few of the rationales that best fit your fact patterns; choose the rationale for which there is the greatest explicit support in the references rather than relying on implicit information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple rationales may apply; however, prefer the rationale(s) most explicitly supported by the references. Avoid relying primarily on implicit inferences if explicit teachings exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofread rejections for internal consistency and completeness
rubrics_metrics.description: Proof read your rejections after writing them to verify that the claims recited in the statement of rejection matches the claims discussed in the body of the rejection, that the references cited to reject dependent claims include all of the references applied to reject any claims from which they depend, and that your overall action is clear and concise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check for matching claim numbers, complete application of references to dependent claims, and clarity in the overall action. Ensure factual support and mapping are present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Level of ordinary skill may be implicit in the record
rubrics_metrics.description: The level of ordinary skill need not always be explicitly stated in the rejection, but may be implicit in view of the record as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the level is clear from the references and evidence in the record, explicit articulation may be unnecessary; nevertheless, ensure the record supports any inference about the skill level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graham factors required in obvious-type double patenting rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Remember that the Graham factors need to be clearly articulated in every 103 obvious double patenting rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the same requirement for clear, reasoned Graham analysis when addressing obvious-type double patenting issues; do not treat double patenting rejections as exceptions to the Graham articulation requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training/rationale list is illustrative, not exhaustive
rubrics_metrics.description: One or more of the rationales set forth in the slides may be relied upon to support a conclusion of obviousness; the list is not intended to be all-inclusive but to provide examples of analyses which meet the necessary burden.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the provided rationales as examples; other rationales or fact patterns may also establish obviousness so long as factual findings and reasoning are provided.
